data.name: Fourtex Jugo
data.detailed_description:
Fourtex Jugo (from the Japanese for "15") is an abstract strategy game with a high degree of difficulty, played on a grid of tiles. Your goal is to optimize each initial layout to beat the target score, and to compete on the leaderboards, or against your personal best score. Progress through each level involves combining three types of particles with each other to ultimately create void. By manipulating the void optimally, you can achieve your goal of meeting or exceeding the target score specified for each particular level, indicating your mastery of that level. For extra challenge, attempt to reach the target score without any particle interaction with the void. You'll need to create your particles and voids at the right times and in the right places to reach your goal.

Key Features

  • Steam features:
    Steam Cloud support
    Big Picture mode: the UI is designed to be easy to see and operate
    Leaderboards (with game playback), Achievements, Trading cards, and Stats

  • Full controller support, or play with keyboard or mouse:
    You can switch input devices automatically, without needing to access a menu.

  • Levels handcrafted by humans:
    Every campaign level is guaranteed playable to 3 stars.

  • Daily levels:
    These levels refresh their initial layouts every 24 hours. They are designed to challenge experienced players, and will play to 3 stars frequently, but not always.

  • Play strategically or casually at your desired level of difficulty:
    Aim for 2 or 3 stars for difficulty ranging all the way up to extremely challenging.
    Play for 1 star for a casual game or while learning the basics.

  • Levels are not locked:
    If you can't master a level yet or it doesn't appeal to you, you can try another one.

  • Original artwork and context-sensitive original audio:
    Audio track is enhanced when voids appear to add dramatic effect.

Game play


There are three tiers of playing pieces (14 number particles, 3 more basic particles, and 2 fundamental particles), each of which combine with themselves, following simple rules, to make another particle or, for the fundamental particles, to make a "void."

The voids provide a turn-based limit to game-play, and the strategy aspect for most of the levels in this game involves correctly timing the creation of voids, and the ability to manipulate these void tiles to both make optimal use of them, and avoid having them grab one of your particles.

How do I win?


The ultimate victory in Jugo is to play all levels to 3 stars, which involves beating a certain target score associated with each level, without any particle interaction with the void tiles. The difficulty of this for a particular level ranges from difficult to extremely challenging.

Another goal for winning a level is to get 2 stars by using the voids effectively, to get even higher scores than are usually possible in a perfect game, and compete for highest score.

This game can also be played as a casual game by simply completing a level to get 1 star.

Not a math puzzle


The most basic tier of particles currently are represented with numbered pieces. The Arabic numerals are a widely recognized sequence, used here to help predict a new particle. Combining similar numbered particles creates the particle with the next highest number, up until 15 (which begins the next tier of 3 more basic particles). A second way to combine the numbered particles is to add particles that have a compatible color hue. But for those who think better with numbers, and for accessibility reasons, these color-compatible pairs also add to 15. The pairs of numbers that add to 15 represent the only math that could be necessary or useful in this game.

reviews.review:
[i]Thank you to the developement team for generously supplying me with a review key.[/i]
---

This review will be in more detail than is probably wanted for potential customers because I want to actually try to help the developer understand why I didn't like it. I would also like to throw ideas on the table with regards to possible improvement.

The mantra any puzzle game should adhere to is [i]easy to learn, impossible to master[/i]. Incredibly, somehow [i]Fourtex Jugo[/i] actually mangages to do the exact [i]opposite[/i]. What we have here is a puzzle mechanic that is based on crafting/building higher-tier icons using more basic elements. There are several tiers of complexity and each has its own rule set. All that is good and fine, but the rules are 1) fairly arbitrary, and 2) don't actually respect other rules. For example, 8+8=9, yet 8+7=pi. And not the mathematical pi that everyone knows; in this universe, pi = 15. Why? No idea. There is also an ohm, but not the physics unit. To complicate things further, the spelling of each of these units is all over the place.

[i]How to fix this problem? Create your own symbols. Our brains will forever connect it with the real, universally accepted symbols. Plus, making your own symbols will further make this game 'your own'. [/i]

I also said the rules are fairly arbitrary. What I mean is that they don't follow any kind of logic pattern that makes them easily remembered. You would do well to actually print out a chart of the rules, otherwise your brain is always working hard to remember these goofy rules. Here is an example of how wonky things get:

[i]8+8=9; 8+7=red pi; red pi+red pi=white ohm; red pi+blue pi (not craftable)=black ohm; black ohm+white ohm = votex. [/i]

Quick! How to make a red pi? To me there is nothing for my brain to grasp onto logically to remember these in any fun way. Like maybe if it was red+pi=red pi. Now that makes sense. You couple this with the fact that there are a metric ton of variables, and its just all very confusing. I'm a smart guy, so it's not that I can't wrap my brain around it - it's just complicated in a way that is not fun to untangle. Here is a brief list of variables: numbers, red pi, blue pi, black ohm, white ohm, vortex, devil hand, tile color, background color, tile shape. Woof.

The design decisions for the UI aren't great either. The puzzle is not centered on the screen. There is unnecessary clutter all over. Just look at the screenshots on the store page. Why do I need all that other stuff? I don't. That top left logo and everything other than the puzzle at hand, and perhaps the score. Check out [i]Hexcells[/i] for good UI design.

Another thing - for being Early Access, the developers aren't all that active on the forums. Let me be clear - they are there, though. Really, at the time of writing this (11/2016), there is only one other active person on the forums other than myself. I've posted about a bug that the developer did address and acknowledge. I've also posted thoughts and, for the most part, have been ignored. Thats fine, but this is Early Access. I guess I just put it in my review.

How does this title manage to be 'impossible to learn, yet easy to master'? Winning a level is absurdly simple. In fact, I've *almost* never lost. There are about ?four tiers to winning. See the store page for details on that. There is no satisfaction, really, when you clear a level because of this. Mind you - I've only 'beaten' a level by the most simple of winning conditions. For the majority of my playtime, we focused on trying to beat the 2000k score for the [i]first[/i] level. We never were able to do it. [i]I mean c'mon what does that tell you?[/i]

The game has a math 'skin' to it, yet really has no math in it. No logic either, other than the obscure ruleset. As I have voiced on the forums to a silent crowd, I think the game would do much better if it were skinned differently. I mean idk, off the top of my head here, how about a fantasy setting where knight+knight=blue army; blue army+white army=civilization. Boom. Solved. It makes *logical* sense, and ends up being more fun at the same time. 

What I did like about the game was that it had good controller support, and good music. The music has little variaty, though. I think there could be a gem here, but it needs an overhaul. I congratulate the developers on the Steam release, which is a major accomplishment in itself. Again, thank you for the free key.

[b]To my Steam friends - I'd wait on this one. It's not ready. [/b]
